candidate.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed p. 12 / PDF p. 16: identify medication adverse effects and provide medication education; monitor/evaluate client response to medication therapy
candidate.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — pregnancy medication safety / sertraline neonatal effects
candidate.educational_objective: Teach that late-pregnancy sertraline exposure can be associated with neonatal respiratory, feeding, and neurologic adaptation symptoms and warrants newborn monitoring without implying that every exposed infant will be severely affected.

options.A: Some exposed newborns have developed findings such as respiratory distress, feeding difficulty, tremor, or jitteriness
options.B: Every exposed newborn will require prolonged intensive-care hospitalization
options.C: Sertraline exposure in late pregnancy has no reported neonatal effects
options.D: The only expected neonatal effect is a congenital limb deformity appearing at birth

candidate.rationale: Current sertraline labeling reports that neonates exposed to sertraline and other SSRIs/SNRIs late in the third trimester have developed complications including respiratory distress, feeding difficulty, tremor, and jitteriness. The label directs clinicians to monitor third-trimester-exposed neonates for persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn and drug discontinuation syndrome. These complications are possible, not inevitable, so B is an unsupported absolute.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Late third-trimester exposure to sertraline can be associated with neonatal respiratory distress, feeding difficulty, tremor, jitteriness and other complications; monitoring is advised.

candidate.stem: A pregnant client taking sertraline asks why the newborn may need observation after third-trimester exposure. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
